summary: Specifies how to make DNS dynamic updates secure, so only authorized parties can add or change records. It uses transaction signatures and keys to authenticate update requests and decide who may change which names. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3007 explains how a DNS server can check who sent a request to change records. The server then applies its own permissions to decide which changes that requester may make.

questions: how to secure dns dynamic updates
what is tsig in dns update
why does dns update use sig0 instead of dnssec sigs
why is update authentication separate from dnssec
subtitle: Secure DNS updates authenticate the requester, then apply the zone administrator's local permissions.

tldr.problem: DNS dynamic update can add and remove records, so a zone needs a way to prevent unauthorized changes.
tldr.mechanism: Each secure update carries TSIG or SIG(0) authentication. The primary server identifies the signer and checks that identity against locally configured policy, which allows no changes by default.
tldr.outcome: Authentication of an update message is separate from DNSSEC signatures on stored data. RFC 3007 obsoletes RFC 2137 and updates RFCs 2136 and 2535.

facts.label: Authentication required
facts.value: TSIG or SIG(0) on each secure update

today: RFC 3007 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2137 and updates RFC 2136 and RFC 2535. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 3007.

sections.title: Securing DNS Dynamic Updates
sections.content:
DNS dynamic update lets a client request record additions or deletions, subject to prerequisites. The request applies to one zone and is processed by that zone's primary server.

RFC 3007 adds authentication to these existing update operations. The primary server must also maintain the zone's SOA serial number when an update occurs or before the next SOA retrieval.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask a zone's primary server to add or remove records. This RFC adds a way for the server to verify who made the request before considering the change.

sections.title: Message Authentication and DNSSEC Data Signatures
sections.content:
TSIG or SIG(0) authenticates the whole update message and can identify its requester. DNSSEC signatures protect records or record sets as zone data, but the RFC explains that they do not adequately protect the structure and prerequisites of an update message.

Once an update changes a signed zone, the changed data must be signed according to the zone's policy. Host or user keys authenticate the request; zone keys authenticate the data stored in DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks a signature on the whole update request to learn who sent it. DNSSEC signatures separately protect the records after the server accepts a change.

sections.title: Identifying the Requester
sections.content:
Every secure dynamic update message MUST contain TSIG or SIG(0). The principal is identified from the key that generated the signature, or from the authenticated TKEY exchange when a shared secret was established dynamically.

An unauthenticated TKEY exchange cannot establish a principal for secure updates. If a key is not authorized, the server MUST return RCODE REFUSED. Ordinary DNSSEC SIG records may appear in a message but must not authenticate the update.
sections.plainLanguage: Every secure update must carry an authentication record that lets the server identify its requester. A key without permission is refused.

sections.title: Local Policy Controls Permissions
sections.content:
The zone administrator configures policy, and the primary name server enforces it. By default, a principal is not permitted to change any zone data; permissions must be enabled in configuration.

Implementations should support rules by name and record type. Normal users should not change SOA or NS records, and dynamic update MUST NOT create, modify, or delete NXT records.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication tells the server who is asking, but local policy decides what that person may change. The default permission list allows no changes.

sections.title: Updates to DNSSEC-Signed Zones
sections.content:
An authorized update may include SIG records, but they are not used to authenticate the request. If an update changes a record set in a signed zone, the set must be signed under the zone's signing policy when processing finishes.

The server may remove signatures that no longer match changed data. If needed, it must generate and sign updated SOA and NXT records as part of the zone's maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing signed DNS data can make its old signature invalid. The server applies the zone's signing policy to the changed records.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Zone keys and other secret material may be held on an online host such as a name server. If an attacker obtains those secrets, DNS data in zones served or delegated by that host may be impersonated.

Allowing updates to KEY records can also create misleading public keys when a requester does not possess the corresponding private key.
sections.plainLanguage: The server must protect its online secret keys. If a requester can add a public key without its private part, others may be misled about who owns it.
